title: Say hello and give your name
goal: Introduce yourself to a new classmate.

objectives.title: Greet, say your name and say goodbye
Use ich bin and ich heiße

cards.title: A name in one sentence
cards.body: A verb is the word that tells what happens or what someone is. Ich means I. Learn two complete name patterns: ich bin and ich heiße. Begin with Hallo when greeting a classmate. Put the name after the verb.

examples.why: Ich is I; bin is the I form of sein, meaning be.
Heiße is the I form of heißen, meaning be called.

cards.title: Choose a name frame
cards.body: Think of ich bin and ich heiße as two empty name badges. Both introduce the speaker. Keep ich and its verb together, then insert a name. A capital letter begins every sentence. End a friendly meeting with Tschüss.

examples.why: Leon fills the name slot after heiße.
Bin gives the name; Tschüss closes the conversation.

references.title: Your first conversation
references.note: Learn Wie heißt du? as one complete question for a classmate. Wie heißt du, Ben? asks Ben his name; Wie heißt du, Anna? asks Anna. The verb heißt stays before du in this question.

terms.meaning: a word such as bin or heiße

watch: Do not say Ich ist Mira. With ich, use bin.

practice.prompt: Which sentence introduces the speaker as Leon?
practice.explanation: Ich bin plus a name identifies the speaker.

practice.prompt: Build: My name is Anna.
practice.explanation: The statement starts with Ich, then heiße, then the name.

practice.prompt: Complete: Ich ___ Mira. Use the verb meaning “am”.
practice.explanation: The I form is bin.

blind.prompt: You play a new character named Ben. Write “Hello! My name is Ben.” Use heiße.
blind.explanation: Hallo greets; Ich heiße introduces the speaker.

retrieval.prompt: Introduce yourself as Leon using bin.
retrieval.explanation: Ich bin plus Leon is the requested introduction.

retrieval.prompt: Introduce yourself as Anna using heiße.
retrieval.explanation: The I form is heiße.

retrieval.prompt: Write “Hello! I am Mira.” Use two sentences.
retrieval.explanation: The greeting and name frame make two short sentences.

reading.title: At the classroom door
reading.text: Hallo! Ich bin Mira. Wie heißt du? Hallo, Mira! Ich heiße Ben. Hallo, Ben! Ich bin Leon. Hallo, Leon! Ich heiße Anna. Hallo, Anna! Ich bin Mira. Tschüss, Ben! Tschüss, Leon! Tschüss, Anna! Tschüss, Mira!
reading.translation: Hello! I am Mira. What is your name? Hello, Mira! My name is Ben. Hello, Ben! I am Leon. Hello, Leon! My name is Anna. Hello, Anna! I am Mira. Bye, Ben! Bye, Leon! Bye, Anna! Bye, Mira!

questions.explanation: The speaker gives the name Ben.
Tschüss closes the meeting.
Wie heißt du? is the name question.

listening.title: A first audio greeting
listening.text: Hallo! Ich heiße Anna. Wie heißt du? Hallo, Anna! Ich bin Leon. Hallo, Leon! Ich bin Ben. Hallo, Ben! Ich heiße Mira. Tschüss, Anna! Tschüss, Leon! Tschüss, Ben!
listening.translation: Hello! My name is Anna. What is your name? Hello, Anna! I am Leon. Hello, Leon! I am Ben. Hello, Ben! My name is Mira. Bye, Anna! Bye, Leon! Bye, Ben!

questions.explanation: The first name sentence is Ich heiße Anna.
The speaker says Leon.
Tschüss means bye.

writing.prompt: You are Anna. Write two short sentences: greet with Hallo, then give your name using bin.
writing.model: Hallo! Ich bin Anna.
writing.hint: Use Hallo! Ich bin + name.
writing.explanation: Ich bin gives the speaker’s name.

prompts: Greet Mira with Hallo.
Introduce yourself as Ben with heiße.
Say goodbye to Leon.

examples.why: Hallo is suitable for a classmate.
Heiße follows ich.

I say the complete phrase clearly.

examples.en: What is your name? My name is Ben.

title: Use du or Sie and ask how someone is
goal: Open and close a polite or friendly conversation.

objectives.title: Ask how someone is and respond
Choose formal Sie or informal du

cards.title: Choose the relationship
cards.body: Du is the familiar you for a friend or classmate. Sie is the polite you for an unfamiliar adult; always capitalize it. The complete how-are-you phrases change too: Wie geht es dir? for du, and Wie geht es Ihnen? for Sie.

examples.de: Hallo, Ben! Wie geht es dir?
examples.why: Dir belongs to the informal phrase used with Ben.

examples.de: Guten Tag, Frau Berg! Wie geht es Ihnen?
examples.en: Good day, Ms Berg! How are you?
examples.why: Ihnen belongs to the polite phrase; the surname supports formal address.

cards.title: Keep each conversation consistent
cards.body: Picture two conversation lanes. In the friendly lane use du, dir and a first name. In the formal lane use Sie, Ihnen and usually Herr or Frau with a surname. A short answer works in both lanes: Danke, gut. Ask back with Und dir? or Und Ihnen?

examples.de: Wie heißt du? – Ich heiße Mira.
examples.en: What is your name? – My name is Mira.
examples.why: The informal name question uses heißt du.

examples.de: Wie heißen Sie? – Ich heiße Leon Berg.
examples.en: What is your name? – My name is Leon Berg.
examples.why: The polite name question uses heißen Sie.

references.title: Greetings and wellbeing
references.note: Gute Nacht is a farewell before sleep, not a normal arrival greeting. Gute Nacht, Ben! closes the evening; Guten Abend, Frau Berg! opens an evening meeting.

watch: Keep the capital in Sie and Ihnen when addressing someone politely.

practice.prompt: You greet an unfamiliar adult. Choose the polite question.
practice.explanation: Ihnen is the formal phrase.

practice.prompt: Build a formal name question.
practice.explanation: Use heißen with formal Sie.

practice.prompt: Complete the friendly return question: Und ___?
practice.explanation: Use Und dir? with a classmate.
practice.hint: The informal phrase ends in dir.

blind.prompt: At a formal evening meeting, greet Ms Berg and ask how she is. Write “Good evening, Ms Berg! How are you?”
answers: Guten Abend, Frau Berg! Wie geht es Ihnen?
blind.explanation: Guten Abend fits evening; Ihnen keeps the formal address.

retrieval.prompt: Ask a friend named Mira “How are you?” Include her name after Hallo.
answers: Hallo, Mira! Wie geht es dir?
retrieval.explanation: A first-name greeting fits dir.

retrieval.prompt: Write the formal farewell “Goodbye, Mr Berg!”
retrieval.explanation: Herr plus surname is formal.

retrieval.prompt: You feel well. Write “Thanks, good. And you?” formally.
retrieval.explanation: Ihnen returns a formal wellbeing question.

reading.title: Two greetings
reading.text: Guten Morgen, Frau Berg! Wie geht es Ihnen? Danke, gut. Und Ihnen? Auch gut, danke. Hallo, Mira! Wie geht es dir? Sehr gut, danke. Und dir? Nicht so gut. Oh! Auf Wiedersehen, Frau Berg! Tschüss, Mira!
reading.translation: Good morning, Ms Berg! How are you? Thanks, good. And you? Also good, thanks. Hello, Mira! How are you? Very good, thanks. And you? Not so good. Oh! Goodbye, Ms Berg! Bye, Mira!

questions.explanation: Guten Morgen, Frau Berg and Ihnen mark formal address.
The answer after Und dir? is Nicht so gut.
Auf Wiedersehen addresses Frau Berg formally.

listening.title: An evening visit
listening.text: Guten Abend, Herr Berg! Ich heiße Anna Wolf. Wie geht es Ihnen? Danke, sehr gut. Und Ihnen? Gut, danke. Hallo, Ben! Wie geht es dir? Gut. Tschüss, Ben! Auf Wiedersehen, Herr Berg!
listening.translation: Good evening, Mr Berg! My name is Anna Wolf. How are you? Thanks, very good. And you? Good, thanks. Hello, Ben! How are you? Good. Bye, Ben! Goodbye, Mr Berg!

questions.explanation: The first words are Guten Abend.
She says Ich heiße Anna Wolf.
Ben receives dir and Tschüss.

writing.prompt: You greet Mr Berg during the day. Write a formal greeting and the formal question asking his name.
answers: Guten Tag, Herr Berg! Wie heißen Sie?
writing.model: Guten Tag, Herr Berg! Wie heißen Sie?
writing.hint: Use Guten Tag and heißen Sie.
writing.explanation: The surname greeting and Sie belong to the same formal lane.

prompts: Greet an adult in the morning.
Ask Ben how he is.
Say you are well and ask back formally.

examples.why: Use Frau with a surname.
Ihnen returns the polite question.

title: Say where you come from and live
goal: Ask and answer origin and home-city questions.

objectives.title: Place the verb in statements and W-questions
Distinguish wo from woher

cards.title: Origin and home are different
cards.body: Woher means from where and asks about origin. Wo means where and asks about a place now. Use kommen aus for origin and wohnen in for your home. A W-question starts with its question word, then the verb, then the person.

examples.de: Woher kommst du? – Ich komme aus Spanien.
examples.en: Where are you from? – I come from Spain.
examples.why: Woher asks origin; aus introduces the country.

examples.de: Wo wohnst du? – Ich wohne in Berlin.
examples.en: Where do you live? – I live in Berlin.
examples.why: Wo asks the current place; in introduces the city.

cards.title: The verb is the hinge
cards.body: Build a statement with the person first and the verb second: ich komme or ich wohne. To ask for a missing detail, put Woher or Wo first and keep the verb next. With du, the endings change to kommst and wohnst.

examples.why: Ich is first and wohne is second; in Wien gives the place.

examples.de: Woher kommen Sie? – Ich komme aus Italien.
examples.en: Where are you from? – I come from Italy.
examples.why: Formal Sie uses kommen; the reply uses ich komme.

references.title: Come and live: present forms
references.note: Wir means we, ihr means familiar plural you, sie means they and Sie means formal you. Wir wohnen in Berlin uses the we form; Ihr kommt aus Spanien uses the familiar plural form. All statements keep the verb second.

references.title: Useful W-questions
references.note: Wer asks identity: Wer bist du? requests a person. Wo asks location: Wo wohnst du? requests a place. Keep the question word before the verb.

terms.meaning: a question beginning with a word such as wo or woher

watch: Do not answer Wo wohnst du? with aus. Say in plus your home city.

practice.prompt: Which question asks origin?
practice.explanation: Woher asks from where.

practice.prompt: Build: I live in Hamburg.
practice.explanation: The verb wohne is second.

practice.prompt: Complete: Du ___ aus Italien.
practice.explanation: Du takes kommst.
practice.hint: Use the du form of kommen.

blind.prompt: Ask a classmate “Where do you live?” Use du and wohnen.
blind.explanation: Wo asks location; wohnst agrees with du.

retrieval.prompt: State “I come from Austria.” Austria = Österreich.
retrieval.explanation: Use komme aus for origin.

retrieval.prompt: Ask formally “Where are you from?”
retrieval.explanation: Formal Sie takes kommen.

retrieval.prompt: State “We live in Vienna.” Vienna = Wien.
retrieval.explanation: Wir takes wohnen; in introduces the city.

reading.title: Three homes
reading.text: Hallo! Ich heiße Leon. Ich komme aus Österreich und wohne in Berlin. Mira kommt aus Spanien. Sie wohnt in Wien. Ben kommt aus Italien und wohnt in Hamburg. Und du? Woher kommst du? Wo wohnst du?
reading.translation: Hello! My name is Leon. I come from Austria and live in Berlin. Mira comes from Spain. She lives in Vienna. Ben comes from Italy and lives in Hamburg. And you? Where are you from? Where do you live?

questions.explanation: Leon says wohne in Berlin.
Mira kommt aus Spanien gives her origin.
The sentence about Ben says wohnt in Hamburg.

listening.title: A registration conversation
listening.text: Guten Tag! Wie heißen Sie? Ich heiße Anna Wolf. Woher kommen Sie? Aus Deutschland. Und wo wohnen Sie? Ich wohne in Zürich. Danke, Frau Wolf. Auf Wiedersehen! Auf Wiedersehen!
listening.translation: Good day! What is your name? My name is Anna Wolf. Where are you from? From Germany. And where do you live? I live in Zurich. Thank you, Ms Wolf. Goodbye! Goodbye!

questions.explanation: She gives Anna Wolf.
She says Ich wohne in Zürich.
The questions use Sie.

writing.prompt: You play Leon. In two sentences say you come from Italy and live in Berlin. Begin both sentences with Ich.
answers: Ich komme aus Italien. Ich wohne in Berlin.
writing.model: Ich komme aus Italien. Ich wohne in Berlin.
writing.hint: Use komme aus, then wohne in.
writing.explanation: Origin and current home use different phrases.

Say you come from Spain.
Ask an unfamiliar adult their origin.

examples.why: Wo asks for a location.
Aus marks origin.

title: Introduce another person
goal: Introduce a friend and replace a repeated name with er or sie.

objectives.title: Use personal pronouns with sein and heißen
Introduce someone else

cards.title: A pronoun replaces a name
cards.body: A personal pronoun is a short word that replaces a person’s name. Use er for he and sie for she. Introduce someone with Das ist plus a name. Then use er or sie and a matching verb instead of repeating the name.

examples.de: Das ist Ben. Er kommt aus Italien.
examples.en: This is Ben. He comes from Italy.
examples.why: Er replaces Ben; kommt is the he form.

examples.de: Das ist Mira. Sie wohnt in Wien.
examples.en: This is Mira. She lives in Vienna.
examples.why: Sie refers back to Mira; wohnt is the she form.

cards.title: Follow the person through the text
cards.body: Imagine an arrow from a name to the next pronoun. A single man can become er and a single woman sie. The verb changes with the pronoun. At a sentence’s start, she and formal you both look like Sie; the conversation tells you which meaning fits.

examples.de: Leon ist neu. Er heißt Leon Wolf.
examples.en: Leon is new. His name is Leon Wolf.
examples.why: Er still means Leon; heißt is the he form of heißen.

examples.de: Anna ist hier. Sie ist neu.
examples.en: Anna is here. She is new.
examples.why: Sie points to Anna; ist agrees with one person.

references.title: Personal pronouns and two key verbs
references.note: Es can refer to a neuter thing; for people here use er or sie as appropriate. Wir sind neu means we are new: sind agrees with we. Ihr seid hier means you all are here: seid agrees with familiar plural you. These are present forms, describing now.

terms.meaning: a short replacement for a name, such as er

watch: Er and sie take ist, not bin: Er ist Ben.

practice.prompt: Replace Mira: Mira wohnt in Berlin.
practice.explanation: Mira becomes sie and the verb stays wohnt.

practice.prompt: Introduce Leon.
practice.explanation: Das ist introduces another person.

practice.prompt: Complete: Wir ___ neu.
practice.explanation: Wir takes sind.

blind.prompt: Introduce Anna with “This is Anna.” Then say “She comes from Spain.”
answers: Das ist Anna. Sie kommt aus Spanien.
blind.explanation: Sie refers to Anna and takes kommt.

retrieval.prompt: Replace Ben in “Ben ist hier.” with the correct pronoun.
retrieval.explanation: Er replaces Ben.

retrieval.prompt: Write “You all are new.” Use familiar plural ihr.
retrieval.explanation: The ihr form of sein is seid.

retrieval.prompt: Introduce Mira, then say she lives in Hamburg. Use Das ist and Sie.
answers: Das ist Mira. Sie wohnt in Hamburg.
retrieval.explanation: Sie replaces Mira and takes wohnt.

reading.title: Meet the new group
reading.text: Das ist Anna. Sie ist neu und kommt aus Deutschland. Sie wohnt in Wien. Das ist Leon. Er kommt aus Österreich und wohnt in Berlin. Mira und Ben sind hier. Sie sind neu. Wir sind auch neu.
reading.translation: This is Anna. She is new and comes from Germany. She lives in Vienna. This is Leon. He comes from Austria and lives in Berlin. Mira and Ben are here. They are new. We are also new.

questions.explanation: Sie wohnt in Wien refers to Anna.

questions.prompt: Who is Er in Er kommt aus Österreich?
questions.explanation: Er follows Das ist Leon.

questions.prompt: What does Sie mean after Mira und Ben?
questions.explanation: Two named people become they, sie.

listening.title: A colleague introduces friends
listening.text: Hallo, Ben! Das ist Mira. Sie kommt aus Italien. Und das ist Leon. Er wohnt in Zürich. Anna ist auch hier. Sie ist neu. Wir sind neu, und ihr seid auch neu. Willkommen!
listening.translation: Hello, Ben! This is Mira. She comes from Italy. And this is Leon. He lives in Zurich. Anna is also here. She is new. We are new, and you all are also new. Welcome!

questions.explanation: Sie kommt aus Italien follows Mira.
Er wohnt in Zürich follows Leon.
Ihr addresses the familiar group.

writing.prompt: Introduce Ben in two sentences. First: “This is Ben.” Second: “He lives in Vienna.” Use a pronoun in sentence two.
answers: Das ist Ben. Er wohnt in Wien.
writing.model: Das ist Ben. Er wohnt in Wien.
writing.hint: The second sentence starts Er.
writing.explanation: Er replaces Ben; wohnt matches one person.

prompts: Introduce Anna.
Say Leon is new using er.
Tell a group of classmates they are here using ihr.

examples.why: Das ist introduces another person.
Ihr requires seid.

title: Countries and languages
goal: Give a short profile with country, city and languages.

objectives.title: Name countries and languages
Use sprechen and fixed country phrases
Recognize Germany, Austria and Switzerland

cards.title: A country is not a language
cards.body: A country answers Woher? A language answers Welche Sprachen? Use Ich komme aus plus a country, and Ich spreche plus a language. Language names begin with capitals. Add und to join two languages. Sprechen changes its vowel with du and er/sie/es.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Frankreich. Ich spreche Französisch.
examples.en: I come from France. I speak French.
examples.why: Frankreich names the country; Französisch names the language.
Ben uses the third-person form spricht; und joins languages.

cards.title: Build a three-part profile
cards.body: Think name, origin, language. Countries and languages have separate labels, even when they look similar. Most country names need no article after aus. Memorize aus der Schweiz, aus der Türkei and aus den USA as whole phrases because these country names use articles.

examples.de: Mira kommt aus der Schweiz. Sie spricht Italienisch.
examples.en: Mira comes from Switzerland. She speaks Italian.
examples.why: Aus der Schweiz is the complete origin phrase; Switzerland has several national languages.

examples.de: Woher kommst du? – Aus den USA. Ich spreche Englisch.
examples.en: Where are you from? – From the USA. I speak English.
examples.why: Aus den USA is the fixed country phrase; Englisch is a language.

references.title: Country and language reference
references.note: This list connects common country and language names; an individual may speak any language. Ich komme aus Japan gives origin. Ich spreche Deutsch gives a language and does not imply German nationality.

references.title: Sprechen and lernen
references.note: Lernen is regular: Ich lerne Deutsch uses lerne after ich. Sprechen changes e to i only with du and er/sie/es: Du sprichst Englisch uses sprichst, not sprechst.

watch: Do not say Ich spreche Deutschland. Deutschland is a country; Deutsch is the language.

practice.prompt: Which word is a language?
practice.explanation: Spanisch is Spanish; Spanien is Spain.

practice.prompt: Build: She speaks German and Italian.
practice.explanation: She uses spricht; languages follow the verb.

practice.prompt: Complete the origin phrase: aus ___ Schweiz.
practice.explanation: Learn aus der Schweiz as a whole phrase.

blind.prompt: Say “I come from Turkey. I speak Turkish.” Use two sentences. Turkey = die Türkei; Turkish = Türkisch.
answers: Ich komme aus der Türkei. Ich spreche Türkisch.
blind.explanation: Use the fixed aus der Türkei phrase and ich spreche.

retrieval.prompt: Write “You speak French.” Use informal singular du.
retrieval.explanation: Du takes sprichst.

retrieval.prompt: Say “We learn German.”
retrieval.explanation: Wir takes lernen.

retrieval.prompt: Say “Ben comes from the USA.”
retrieval.explanation: The complete origin phrase is aus den USA.

reading.title: Language partners
reading.text: Mira kommt aus der Schweiz und wohnt in Lugano. Sie spricht Italienisch und Deutsch. Ben kommt aus Brasilien. Er spricht Portugiesisch und lernt Deutsch. Anna kommt aus Österreich. Sie spricht Deutsch und Englisch. Wir lernen zusammen Deutsch.
reading.translation: Mira comes from Switzerland and lives in Lugano. She speaks Italian and German. Ben comes from Brazil. He speaks Portuguese and learns German. Anna comes from Austria. She speaks German and English. We learn German together.

questions.explanation: Ben lernt Deutsch.
Anna kommt aus Österreich.
Mira spricht Italienisch und Deutsch.

listening.title: An interview at the course
listening.text: Wie heißt du? Ich heiße Leon. Woher kommst du? Aus Frankreich. Welche Sprachen sprichst du? Ich spreche Französisch und Englisch. Lernst du Deutsch? Ja, ich lerne Deutsch. Und du? Ich komme aus Japan.
listening.translation: What is your name? My name is Leon. Where are you from? From France. Which languages do you speak? I speak French and English. Are you learning German? Yes, I am learning German. And you? I come from Japan.

questions.explanation: He answers Aus Frankreich.
He says Französisch und Englisch.
He says Ja, ich lerne Deutsch.

writing.prompt: You are Mira from Switzerland. Write two sentences: your origin with Ich komme; your languages German and French with Ich spreche.
answers: Ich komme aus der Schweiz. Ich spreche Deutsch und Französisch.
writing.model: Ich komme aus der Schweiz. Ich spreche Deutsch und Französisch.
writing.hint: Use aus der Schweiz and join languages with und.
writing.explanation: Both sentences use the ich verb form.

prompts: Name your role’s country: Japan.
Ask Ben which languages he speaks.
Say you learn German.

examples.why: Du takes sprichst.
The language follows lerne.

title: Spell names and exchange contact details
goal: Give a phone number and spell an email address.

objectives.title: Name alphabet letters and email symbols
Use numbers zero to twenty
Repeat and confirm contact details

cards.title: Contact details need small chunks
cards.body: Give a phone number one digit at a time so the listener can write it accurately. For an email address, pronounce symbols too: @ is ät, a dot is Punkt, a hyphen is minus and an underscore is Unterstrich. Spell an unclear name letter by letter.

examples.de: Meine Telefonnummer ist null eins sieben zwei.
examples.en: My telephone number is zero one seven two.
examples.why: Individual digit names avoid confusion in a phone number.

examples.de: ben Punkt wolf ät example Punkt com
examples.why: Punkt marks each dot and ät marks @.

cards.title: Say it, check it, repeat it
cards.body: Think of a contact detail as a sequence of separate pieces. Pause between digit groups or email parts. If you miss a piece, ask Noch einmal, bitte. To spell a name, use German letter names rather than reading the name as a word.

examples.why: Say em, ee, err, ah: these are letter names, not English spelling.

examples.de: Wie bitte? Noch einmal, bitte: null neun acht.
examples.en: Pardon? Once again, please: zero nine eight.
examples.why: Requesting repetition lets you confirm the same digits.

references.title: Numbers 0–20
references.note: 13–19 mostly combine a unit and zehn; 16 shortens sechs to sech-, and 17 shortens sieben to sieb-. Sechzehn means 16 with no s before zehn. Siebzehn means 17 with no en before zehn. Phone digits use eins, not ein.

references.title: German alphabet: letter names
references.note: These are approximate English-friendly letter names, not spelling rules for whole words. W is called veh: spell WOLF beginning veh, oh. V is called fow: spell EVA ending fow, ah. Keep W and V distinct.

references.title: Email and repair phrases
references.note: Read every symbol in its position. mira_ben says mira Unterstrich ben because _ is an underscore. leon-wolf says leon minus wolf because - is a hyphen.

watch: In a phone number, zero is null. Do not omit it at the beginning.

practice.prompt: What does ben Unterstrich wolf represent?
practice.explanation: Unterstrich names _.

practice.prompt: Put the digit names for 0 1 8 in order.
practice.explanation: Read digits in their written order.

practice.prompt: Write the German word for 17.
practice.explanation: Siebzehn loses the en from sieben.

blind.prompt: Write the email address you hear: “mira minus ben ät example Punkt de”. Enter only the address.
blind.explanation: Minus is -, ät is @, and Punkt is a dot.

retrieval.prompt: Write 16 as one German word.
retrieval.explanation: Sechzehn has no s before zehn.

retrieval.prompt: Write the digits you hear: null sieben zwei neun. Enter digits only.
retrieval.explanation: Keep the initial zero.

retrieval.prompt: Write the email: leon Unterstrich wolf ät example Punkt com. Address only.
retrieval.explanation: Unterstrich becomes _; ät becomes @.

reading.title: A contact card
reading.text: Hallo, ich heiße Mira Wolf. Ich wohne in Berlin und lerne Deutsch. Meine Telefonnummer ist null eins sieben acht zwei neun. Meine E-Mail-Adresse ist mira Punkt wolf ät example Punkt de. Mein Name: M – I – R – A. Danke!
reading.translation: Hello, my name is Mira Wolf. I live in Berlin and am learning German. My telephone number is zero one seven eight two nine. My email address is mira dot wolf at example dot de. My name: M – I – R – A. Thank you!

questions.prompt: Which number is on the card?
questions.explanation: The digits are null eins sieben acht zwei neun.
Punkt follows mira and example; the ending is de.
The letters M–I–R–A spell Mira.

glossary.en: my, used here with Telefonnummer and E-Mail-Adresse

listening.title: Confirming a number
listening.text: Wie ist deine Telefonnummer, Ben? Null eins sechs vier acht. Wie bitte? Noch einmal, bitte. Null eins sechs vier acht. Danke. Und deine E-Mail-Adresse? Ben Unterstrich leon ät example Punkt com. Bitte buchstabieren: B – E – N.
listening.translation: What is your phone number, Ben? Zero one six four eight. Pardon? Once again, please. Zero one six four eight. Thanks. And your email address? Ben underscore leon at example dot com. Please spell: B – E – N.

questions.explanation: The order is null eins sechs vier acht.

questions.prompt: What symbol separates ben and leon?
questions.explanation: Unterstrich means underscore.

questions.prompt: Why is Noch einmal, bitte said?
questions.explanation: It asks the speaker to repeat.

writing.prompt: Write a two-sentence contact message for Ben: “My name is Ben.” Then “My telephone number is 0173.” Use German digit words in the second sentence.

title: Talk about hobbies
goal: Say what you and a friend enjoy doing.

objectives.title: Describe hobbies with gern
Conjugate regular verbs and lesen

cards.title: An activity you enjoy
cards.body: Gern means that you like doing an activity. Put it after the verb in these short statements. A regular verb loses its infinitive ending -en and gets a person ending. Lesen is irregular: its vowel changes to ie with du and er/sie/es.

examples.why: Koche agrees with ich; gern adds enjoyment.

cards.title: Change the person, keep the hobby
cards.body: Start with the dictionary action, such as kochen. Match its ending to the person: ich koche, du kochst, wir kochen. Gern still expresses enjoyment. Learn liest as one sound for both du and er/sie/es; do not create an extra syllable.

examples.why: Wir takes spielen; Fußball names the activity.

references.title: Hobby verbs: present
references.note: Arbeiten inserts an e before -st and -t to make the ending pronounceable: Du arbeitest, not arbeitst. Ihr arbeitet uses the same extra e. Regular hobbies include spielen, reisen, schwimmen, singen, joggen, hören and fotografieren; tanzen uses du tanzt because its stem already ends in z.

references.title: Enjoyment and hobbies
references.note: Nicht gern negates enjoyment: Ich singe nicht gern means I do not like singing. Ich reise gern means I like traveling. Treat ins Kino as one destination phrase for now.

terms.meaning: the dictionary verb form, such as kochen

title: Arrange a day to meet
goal: Suggest a shared activity and agree on a weekday.

objectives.title: Ask yes/no questions with the verb first

cards.title: A question without a W-word
cards.body: A yes/no question can be answered with ja or nein. Put the verb first, then the person. To suggest a shared plan, use Gehen wir …? or Spielen wir …? Give a weekday with am. Say Ja, gern to accept or Das geht leider nicht to decline.

examples.en: Shall we play football on Monday?
examples.why: Spielen comes first because this is a yes/no suggestion.

examples.de: Gehst du am Freitag ins Kino?
examples.en: Are you going to the cinema on Friday?
examples.why: Gehst comes before du; am Freitag names the day.

cards.title: Turn the statement around
cards.body: Imagine swapping only the first two pieces. Du spielst becomes Spielst du? and Wir gehen becomes Gehen wir? In a neutral yes/no question the voice often rises at the end. An answer normally falls. W-questions commonly fall too; intonation supports the word order.

examples.why: The verb moves before du to form the question; let the question rise.

examples.de: Gehen wir am Dienstag ins Kino? – Ja, gern.
examples.en: Shall we go to the cinema on Tuesday? – Yes, gladly.
examples.why: The suggestion rises; the completed answer falls.

references.title: The week
references.note: Weekdays are masculine nouns; learn der Montag, die Montage and the same plural -e for the other weekdays. Am Montag means on Monday, while von Montag bis Freitag means from Monday to Friday. Am Sonntag schwimme ich names a day; Ich arbeite von Montag bis Freitag gives a range.

references.title: Making plans and voice patterns
references.note: Wann asks when: Wann schwimmst du? requests a day or time and often falls. Schwimmst du am Freitag? checks a plan, can receive yes/no and often rises.

watch: Do not keep statement order in a neutral yes/no question: Spielst du …?, not Du spielst …?

title: Jobs and working hours
goal: Describe a job and a simple work schedule.

objectives.title: Talk about profession and working hours
Use sein and haben present forms

cards.title: Be a professional, have a schedule
cards.body: Use sein to name a profession: Ich bin Lehrer. Normally omit an article when simply stating a job. Use haben for what you have, including time or a day off. Haben is irregular with du and er/sie/es. Say hours with von … bis … Uhr.

examples.de: Mira ist Lehrerin. Sie arbeitet von acht bis zwölf Uhr.
examples.en: Mira is a teacher. She works from eight until twelve.
examples.why: Ist names the profession; von … bis … gives the work period.
Hat is the he form of haben; frei haben means have time off.

cards.title: Choose be or have
cards.body: Ask whether your sentence identifies someone or says what they have. A job answers Was bist du von Beruf? A free day answers Wann hast du frei? With an hour range, place von before the starting hour and bis before the ending hour; say Uhr at the end.

examples.de: Ich bin Kellner. Ich habe am Dienstag frei.
examples.en: I am a waiter. I have Tuesday off.
examples.why: Bin identifies the job; habe introduces time off.

examples.de: Wir arbeiten von neun bis fünfzehn Uhr.
examples.en: We work from nine until fifteen hundred hours.
examples.why: The range starts at 9 and ends at 15; formal hours can exceed twelve.

references.title: Be and have: all present forms
references.note: Du hast am Freitag frei uses hast with du. Ihr habt am Sonntag frei uses habt with familiar plural you. Sein is also irregular: Wir sind Lehrer uses sind; Ihr seid Lehrer uses seid.

references.title: Professions and time phrases
references.note: Many feminine job names add -in; plural often ends -innen: Lehrerin → Lehrerinnen. Anna ist Ärztin names one woman doctor. Ben ist Arzt names one man doctor. Use the actual person’s job title; the suffix is a vocabulary pattern, not a universal rule.

title: Learn nouns with articles and plurals
goal: Identify everyday work objects and make useful noun flashcards.

objectives.title: Use der, das, die and common plural patterns
Learn each noun with its article and plural

cards.title: A noun has a partner
cards.body: A noun names a person, place or thing. German nouns begin with capitals and have a grammatical gender: der, das or die. The gender often cannot be guessed from meaning. Learn the article with the noun and record the plural, the form for more than one.

examples.de: Das Buch ist hier. Die Bücher sind hier.
examples.en: The book is here. The books are here.
examples.why: Buch has das; its plural changes u to ü and adds -er. All plural articles here are die.

examples.de: Der Stift ist hier. Die Stifte sind hier.
examples.en: The pen is here. The pens are here.
examples.why: Stift has der; its plural adds -e and uses die.

cards.title: Make a three-piece memory card
cards.body: Store an article, a singular noun and its full plural together. Sort cards into der, das and die groups, or imagine the objects in three places. Cover one side and recall the whole phrase aloud. A plural may change its ending, vowel, both or neither.

examples.why: The noun adds -n; say the article and both full forms.
This plural adds -s; do not assume every noun uses -s.

references.title: Common plural shapes
references.note: These are patterns to recognize, not rules that predict every noun. Der Schlüssel becomes die Schlüssel with no ending. Die Rechnung becomes die Rechnungen with -en. Copy the full dictionary plural rather than guessing from English.

references.title: Read a noun entry
references.note: Buch, das, Bücher tells you das Buch and die Bücher. Rechnung, die, -en tells you die Rechnung and die Rechnungen: attach -en to the singular. Our vocabulary cards display full plurals to reduce decoding.

watch: A noun’s plural always uses die in this basic naming form, even if its singular uses der or das.

practice.explanation: It records article, capitalized noun and correct plural.

practice.explanation: Plural Stifte uses die and sind.

retrieval.explanation: Singular Buch uses das and ist.

title: Read numbers above twenty
goal: Understand ages, quantities and larger numbers in work profiles.

objectives.title: Build numbers from twenty-one through one thousand and recognize larger scales

cards.title: Say units before tens
cards.body: For numbers from 21 to 99, say the unit first, then und, then the ten. Write the whole number as one word. Use ein, not eins, inside einundzwanzig. Exact tens have no und. Learn the special tens dreißig, sechzig and siebzig carefully.

examples.why: Say four-and-twenty: unit, und, ten.
One becomes ein inside the compound; dreißig has ß.

cards.title: Read a number in blocks
cards.body: Split a written number into hundreds, then the remaining tens and units. Say the hundred block first. Inside the last two digits, reverse the order to units-und-tens. Einhundert and hundert both mean 100. A standalone one remains eins.

examples.why: Read 200 first, then six-and-forty for 46.
Ein joins tausend; tausend alone is also possible.

references.title: Number-building reference
rows: einundzwanzig, zweiundzwanzig, dreiundzwanzig, vierundzwanzig, fünfundzwanzig, sechsundzwanzig, siebenundzwanzig, achtundzwanzig, neunundzwanzig
zweihundert, dreihundert, vierhundert, fünfhundert, sechshundert, siebenhundert, achthundert, neunhundert
references.note: Numbers below a million are written together: 1250 is eintausendzweihundertfünfzig, meaning 1000 + 200 + 50. Million and Milliarde are nouns and stay separate and capitalized: zwei Millionen means 2,000,000, adding plural -en. Eine Milliarde equals one billion in English, not one million.

references.title: Numbers in context
rows: Ich arbeite vierzig Stunden pro Woche.

title: Fill in a club registration
goal: Match personal details to a registration form and ask for missing information.

objectives.title: Complete personal-information fields
Check names, address and contact details
Read a sports-club registration

cards.title: A form uses labels
cards.body: A form often uses noun labels instead of full questions. Vorname means given name; Nachname or Familienname means surname. Wohnort is the town where you live; Geburtsort is where you were born. Match each label to the correct detail before copying anything.

examples.why: Two separate fields divide a full name.

examples.en: Place of residence: Berlin. Place of birth: Vienna.
examples.why: A current home and a birthplace can be different.

cards.title: Check one field at a time
cards.body: Read the label first, find the matching detail, then copy it exactly. German dates on forms usually use day, month, year as numbers. A postal code belongs with a town; a house number belongs with a street. Ask a taught W-question when a detail is missing.

examples.why: 08 is the day and 04 is the month, not August fourth.
The house number follows the street; the postal code precedes the town.

references.title: Registration labels
references.note: On a form, a label and value can replace a full sentence. Kurs: Tennis identifies the activity without a verb. Tag: Freitag selects Friday without am because it is a label, not a sentence.

references.title: Ask for a missing detail
references.note: Ihre means your in these formal feminine noun phrases. Wie ist Ihre Telefonnummer? asks for a phone number. Wie ist Ihre E-Mail-Adresse? asks for an email address; both keep the polite capital I.

watch: Geburtsort is birthplace; do not automatically copy your current Wohnort there.

practice.prompt: Which field needs Wolf in Ben Wolf?
practice.explanation: Wolf is the surname.

practice.prompt: Build a formal question asking the home city.
practice.explanation: Wo requests the place; wohnen agrees with Sie.

practice.prompt: In 09.03.2002, which month number is written? Enter two digits.
practice.explanation: German numeric forms normally put day first, then month.
practice.hint: The middle group is the month.

blind.prompt: A form says: full name Leon Berg, home city Hamburg. Write the three fields exactly in this order: Vorname: …; Nachname: …; Wohnort: …
answers: Vorname: Leon; Nachname: Berg; Wohnort: Hamburg
blind.explanation: Given name, surname and current home match separate labels.

retrieval.explanation: Wolf is the surname.

retrieval.explanation: A labeled field does not need a verb.

retrieval.explanation: Use Ihre with E-Mail-Adresse.

reading.title: Joining a sports club
reading.text: Ben Wolf wohnt in Hamburg. Er kommt aus Österreich. Sein Geburtsort ist Wien. Er ist vierundzwanzig Jahre alt. Im Sportclub lernt er Tennis. Der Kurs ist am Samstag. Ben schreibt seinen Vornamen, Nachnamen und Wohnort in das Formular.
reading.translation: Ben Wolf lives in Hamburg. He comes from Austria. His birthplace is Vienna. He is twenty-four years old. At the sports club he learns tennis. The course is on Saturday. Ben writes his given name, surname and place of residence in the form.

questions.explanation: Ben currently lives in Hamburg.
Im Sportclub lernt er Tennis.
Der Kurs ist am Samstag.

listening.title: At the club desk
listening.text: Guten Tag! Der Yoga-Kurs ist am Freitag. Wie heißen Sie? Ich heiße Mira Berg. Wo wohnen Sie? In Berlin. Und Ihre Telefonnummer? Null eins sieben drei acht. Danke. Ihr Vorname ist Mira, Ihr Nachname ist Berg.
listening.translation: Good day! The yoga course is on Friday. What is your name? My name is Mira Berg. Where do you live? In Berlin. And your phone number? Zero one seven three eight. Thank you. Your given name is Mira, your surname is Berg.

questions.explanation: The first sentence says am Freitag.
The final sentence confirms Nachname ist Berg.
Keep null, then eins sieben drei acht.

writing.prompt: For Anna Wolf, who lives in Wien, write two sentences: her name using Sie heißt, then her home using Sie wohnt.
answers: Sie heißt Anna Wolf. Sie wohnt in Wien.
writing.model: Sie heißt Anna Wolf. Sie wohnt in Wien.
writing.hint: Sie refers to Anna; use heißt and wohnt.
writing.explanation: The sentences supply name and home details for a form.

title: Identify places in town
goal: Introduce a place and then describe the same place.

objectives.title: Choose ein/eine, then der/das/die for a known place
Describe a place with sein and an unchanged adjective
Name essential buildings and sights

cards.title: First a place, then the place
cards.body: An article is the small partner before a noun. Use ein or eine for a new, unidentified place. Once the place is known, use der, das or die. Masculine and neuter nouns take ein; feminine nouns take eine. For several new things there is no indefinite article.

examples.de: Das ist ein Hafen. Der Hafen ist groß.
examples.en: That is a port. The port is big.
examples.why: Hafen is masculine: introduce it with ein, then refer back with der.

examples.de: Das ist eine Kirche. Die Kirche ist schön.
examples.en: That is a church. The church is beautiful.
examples.why: Kirche is feminine: first eine, then die.

cards.title: Identify, then add a description
cards.body: Think of a two-step camera shot: first identify the object, then zoom in on it. After sein, an adjective, a describing word, keeps its dictionary form. A plural uses sind. The adjective does not get a plural ending in this pattern.

examples.de: Das ist ein Hotel. Das Hotel ist neu.
examples.en: That is a hotel. The hotel is new.
examples.why: Hotel is neuter; neu follows ist without an ending.

examples.de: Das sind Brücken. Die Brücken sind schön.
examples.en: Those are bridges. The bridges are beautiful.
examples.why: The new plural has no ein; the known plural uses die and sind.

references.title: Introducing and referring back
references.note: Das ist ein Rathaus introduces a town hall as one new object. Das Rathaus ist alt then describes that same town hall. With a plural use Das sind Museen, not Das ist Museen.

references.title: A town vocabulary map
references.note: These place names can answer Was ist das? Der See ist groß describes a lake; Der Fluss ist lang describes a river. Adjectives after ist have no extra ending.

terms.meaning: small word such as ein or der before a noun
a describing word such as groß

watch: Say Das ist eine Kirche, but Das ist ein Hotel. Learn each noun’s gender.

practice.prompt: You identify a church for the first time. Choose the sentence.
practice.explanation: Kirche is feminine and singular, so use eine and ist.

practice.prompt: Build: The station is big.
practice.explanation: Use der with Bahnhof and leave groß unchanged.

practice.prompt: Complete: Das sind ___ . Write the full plural noun for Museum without an article.
practice.explanation: The plural of Museum is Museen; new plurals need no indefinite article.

blind.prompt: Identify a theatre and then describe it as beautiful. Write two sentences using Das ist first. Theatre = das Theater; beautiful = schön.
answers: Das ist ein Theater. Das Theater ist schön.
blind.explanation: Use ein for a new neuter noun, then das for the known theatre.

retrieval.prompt: Identify one new town hall: “That is a town hall.”
retrieval.explanation: Rathaus is neuter and takes ein.

retrieval.prompt: Describe the known bridges as big. Begin Die Brücken.
retrieval.explanation: Plural uses sind; groß stays unchanged.

retrieval.prompt: Identify several new hotels: “Those are hotels.”
retrieval.explanation: Plural takes sind and no indefinite article.

reading.title: A walk with Mira
reading.text: Mira ist in Hamburg. Das ist ein Hafen. Der Hafen ist groß. Hier ist eine Brücke. Die Brücke ist schön. Dort ist ein Museum. Das Museum ist neu. Ben fragt: Ist das eine Kirche? Nein, das ist das Rathaus.
reading.translation: Mira is in Hamburg. That is a port. The port is big. Here is a bridge. The bridge is beautiful. Over there is a museum. The museum is new. Ben asks: Is that a church? No, that is the town hall.

questions.prompt: Which place is described as big?
questions.explanation: Der Hafen ist groß.
Das Museum ist neu.

questions.prompt: Is Ben looking at a church?
options: No, it is the town hall
questions.explanation: The correction is Nein, das ist das Rathaus.

listening.title: Looking from the square
listening.text: Was ist das, Anna? Das ist ein Bahnhof. Ist der Bahnhof neu? Nein, der Bahnhof ist alt. Und hier? Das sind Hotels. Die Hotels sind groß. Dort ist eine Kirche. Die Kirche ist schön.
listening.translation: What is that, Anna? That is a station. Is the station new? No, the station is old. And here? Those are hotels. The hotels are big. Over there is a church. The church is beautiful.

questions.explanation: Der Bahnhof ist alt.

questions.prompt: Are there one or several hotels?
questions.explanation: Das sind Hotels is plural.
Die Kirche ist schön.

writing.prompt: Identify one new square, then describe the same square as big. Use Das ist and two sentences. Square = der Platz.
answers: Das ist ein Platz. Der Platz ist groß.
writing.model: Das ist ein Platz. Der Platz ist groß.
writing.hint: Start ein Platz; refer back with der Platz.
writing.explanation: The first article introduces the square; the second identifies it.

Identify a museum.
Describe the museum as beautiful.

examples.why: The W-question starts with Was.
Schön has no adjective ending after ist.

title: Correct an identification and name transport
goal: Say what a vehicle is and what it is not.

objectives.title: Use kein/keine for a negative noun identification
Identify eight common means of transport

cards.title: A negative article says not a
cards.body: Kein is a negative article: it denies that something is a member of a noun category. It replaces ein. Use kein with masculine or neuter singular nouns, and keine with feminine or plural nouns. Keep ist for one thing and sind for several.

examples.de: Das ist kein Bus. Das ist ein Zug.
examples.en: That is not a bus. That is a train.
examples.why: Bus is masculine, so the negative article is kein.

examples.de: Das ist keine U-Bahn. Das ist eine S-Bahn.
examples.en: That is not an underground train. That is a suburban train.
examples.why: Both transport words are feminine; the negative article is keine.

cards.title: Correct the label in two steps
cards.body: First reject the wrong category, then give the correct category. The article matches the noun after it, even when both nouns describe the same object. In the plural, use keine for all genders. Kein is useful for a noun; nicht is useful for negating a description.

examples.de: Das ist kein Auto. Das ist ein Fahrrad.
examples.en: That is not a car. That is a bicycle.
examples.why: Auto and Fahrrad are neuter and both use ein or kein.

examples.de: Das sind keine Schiffe. Das sind Flugzeuge.
examples.en: Those are not ships. Those are aeroplanes.
examples.why: Plural negative is keine; positive new plural has no article.

references.title: Positive and negative identification
rows: keine Busse / keine Autos / keine U-Bahnen
references.note: Das ist keine Brücke denies the noun category bridge. Die Brücke ist nicht neu negates the description new. Do not combine ein with kein: choose one article.

references.title: Transport reference
references.note: U-Bahn and S-Bahn are different transport labels; learn each abbreviation with die. Das ist eine S-Bahn names one vehicle or service. Das sind Züge names several trains.

watch: Do not say Das ist nicht ein Bus for this basic category correction. Use Das ist kein Bus.

practice.prompt: Choose “Those are not cars.”
practice.explanation: Plural needs sind and keine.

practice.prompt: Build: That is not an underground train.
practice.explanation: U-Bahn is feminine; use keine.

practice.prompt: Complete: Das ist ___ Fahrrad. Meaning: That is not a bicycle.
practice.explanation: Fahrrad is neuter; use kein.

blind.prompt: Correct a vehicle label: “That is not a train. That is a ship.” Use two sentences. Train = der Zug; ship = das Schiff.
answers: Das ist kein Zug. Das ist ein Schiff.
blind.explanation: Zug takes kein; Schiff takes ein.

retrieval.prompt: Say “That is not an aeroplane.”
retrieval.explanation: Flugzeug is neuter.

retrieval.prompt: Say “Those are not buses.”
retrieval.explanation: Busse is the plural; use sind and keine.

retrieval.prompt: Say “The car is not new.”
retrieval.explanation: Nicht negates the adjective neu; kein would negate a noun.

reading.title: At a transport display
reading.text: Ben und Mira sind im Museum. Ben fragt: Ist das ein Bus? Mira sagt: Nein, das ist kein Bus. Das ist eine S-Bahn. Hier sind Fahrräder. Dort ist ein Schiff. Das Schiff ist alt. Die Fahrräder sind neu.
reading.translation: Ben and Mira are in the museum. Ben asks: Is that a bus? Mira says: No, that is not a bus. That is a suburban train. Here are bicycles. Over there is a ship. The ship is old. The bicycles are new.

questions.prompt: What does Ben first mistake for a bus?
questions.explanation: Mira corrects him: Das ist eine S-Bahn.
Das Schiff ist alt.
Die Fahrräder sind neu.

listening.title: A photo conversation
listening.text: Ist das ein Flugzeug, Leon? Nein, das ist kein Flugzeug. Das ist ein Schiff. Und hier, ist das ein Auto? Ja, genau. Die Autos sind klein. Das sind keine Busse. Die Busse sind dort.
listening.translation: Is that an aeroplane, Leon? No, that is not an aeroplane. That is a ship. And here, is that a car? Yes, exactly. The cars are small. Those are not buses. The buses are over there.

questions.prompt: What is the first vehicle actually?
questions.explanation: Das ist ein Schiff corrects the first guess.
Die Autos sind klein.
Die Busse sind dort.

writing.prompt: Correct two plural labels: say “Those are not ships. Those are buses.”
answers: Das sind keine Schiffe. Das sind Busse.
writing.model: Das sind keine Schiffe. Das sind Busse.
writing.hint: The negative plural needs keine; the positive new plural has no article.
writing.explanation: Both plural clauses use sind.

prompts: Ask whether an object is a bicycle.
Correct the label: it is a car.
Say that several objects are not trains.

examples.why: The yes/no question starts with ist.
Nein introduces the correction.

title: Ask for and follow a short route
goal: Ask politely for a destination and confirm two route steps.

objectives.title: Ask for a place, give directions and confirm a route
Use a polite instruction with verb plus Sie
Use left, right, straight on, here, there and then

cards.title: A polite route starts with an instruction
cards.body: An instruction tells someone what to do. For a polite instruction, put the full verb first, then Sie. Add a direction after Sie. Begin a request with Entschuldigung. Ask Wo ist bitte plus the destination; the article stays with the place name.

examples.de: Entschuldigung, wo ist bitte der Bahnhof?
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station, please?
examples.why: Wo requests a location; der belongs to Bahnhof.

examples.de: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann rechts.
examples.en: Go straight on and then right.
examples.why: Gehen Sie is the polite walking instruction; dann orders the second step.

cards.title: Repeat the route before you walk
cards.body: Break a route into one or two actions. Listen for links, rechts and geradeaus. Repeat the actions with Also …? to check them. Genau confirms your understanding. Finish with Vielen Dank. For a driver, Fahren Sie uses the same polite verb-first pattern.

examples.de: Also hier links und dann geradeaus? – Ja, genau.
examples.en: So left here and then straight on? – Yes, exactly.
examples.why: The repeated order checks both direction and sequence.

examples.en: Drive right. – Thank you very much!
examples.why: Fahren comes before Sie in the polite instruction.

references.title: Direction words and useful phrases
references.note: Gehen Sie links tells someone to walk left. Fahren Sie geradeaus tells someone to continue straight by vehicle. In both instructions, Sie follows the verb; use a capital S.

references.title: A route in small steps
rows: Gehen Sie rechts und dann links.
references.note: Also rechts und dann links? repeats a route as a checking question. Ja, genau confirms that sequence. If a word is unclear, say Noch einmal, bitte before leaving.

terms.meaning: a verb pattern used for instructions

watch: In a polite instruction say Gehen Sie, not Sie gehen. Keep route steps in the order you heard.

practice.prompt: A helper says geradeaus, dann links. What do you do?
practice.explanation: Dann puts the left turn after the straight section.

practice.prompt: Build the polite instruction “Go right.”
practice.explanation: The instruction has verb first, then capitalized Sie.

practice.prompt: Complete the polite question: Entschuldigung, ___ ist bitte das Hotel?
practice.explanation: Wo asks for a place.

blind.prompt: Tell a stranger to walk left and then right. Start Gehen Sie.
answers: Gehen Sie links und dann rechts.
blind.explanation: The polite instruction begins with Gehen Sie and preserves left-then-right order.

retrieval.prompt: Ask politely “Where is the church, please?” Begin Wo and use die Kirche.
retrieval.explanation: Die Kirche is the destination in a Wo-question.

retrieval.prompt: Tell a driver “Drive straight on.” Use polite Sie.
retrieval.explanation: Fahren Sie is a polite instruction for travel by vehicle.

retrieval.prompt: Check “So straight on here and then left?” Use Also hier.
answers: Also hier geradeaus und dann links?
retrieval.explanation: The checking phrase repeats the two actions in order.

reading.title: Finding the theatre
reading.text: Anna fragt: Entschuldigung, wo ist bitte das Theater? Ein Mann sagt: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann links. Da ist das Theater. Anna fragt: Also geradeaus und dann links? Ja, genau. Anna sagt: Vielen Dank! Der Mann sagt: Bitte, gern.
reading.translation: Anna asks: Excuse me, where is the theatre, please? A man says: Go straight on and then left. The theatre is there. Anna asks: So straight on and then left? Yes, exactly. Anna says: Thank you very much! The man says: You are welcome.

questions.prompt: Where does Anna want to go?
questions.explanation: She asks wo ist bitte das Theater.
The helper starts Gehen Sie geradeaus.

questions.prompt: Why does Anna repeat the route?
questions.explanation: Her Also-question repeats the two directions.

listening.title: Directions to the hotel
listening.text: Entschuldigung, wo ist bitte das Hotel? Gehen Sie hier rechts und dann geradeaus. Also rechts, dann geradeaus? Ja, genau. Dort ist das Hotel. Vielen Dank! Bitte, gern. Das Hotel ist groß und neu.
listening.translation: Excuse me, where is the hotel, please? Go right here and then straight on. So right, then straight on? Yes, exactly. The hotel is over there. Thank you very much! You are welcome. The hotel is big and new.

questions.explanation: The first question names das Hotel.
The route starts hier rechts.
The helper says dann geradeaus.

writing.prompt: Give a two-step walking route: straight on, then right. Use one polite sentence beginning Gehen Sie.
answers: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann rechts.
writing.model: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann rechts.
writing.hint: Put Sie after Gehen; connect the directions with und dann.
writing.explanation: The instruction orders the requested route steps.

prompts: Ask politely for the station.
Give a left-then-straight walking route.
Repeat that route to check it, then thank the helper.

examples.why: The question requests one place.

examples.de: Gehen Sie links und dann geradeaus.
examples.en: Go left and then straight on.
examples.why: The two directions follow the route order.

I say the two steps in the right order.
I use a checking phrase or a thank-you.

The station is on the right.
Excuse me, where is the hotel?

title: Use months and seasons
goal: Say when you do a familiar activity using a month or season.

objectives.title: Name all twelve months and four seasons
Use im with a month or season
Connect D-A-CH seasons with everyday activities

cards.title: A month or season answers when
cards.body: Use im before a month or season: im Mai, im Sommer. Use am before a weekday: am Freitag. Month and season names begin with capitals. Keep a simple activity sentence: person, verb, time. Im is a whole useful time phrase here.

examples.why: A month takes im; Juli names July.
A season also takes im; Herbst means autumn.

cards.title: Build a calendar in small groups
cards.body: Learn months in four groups of three, then connect them to seasons. For this simple Central European calendar, March to May is spring, June to August summer, September to November autumn, and December to February winter. Review by covering one group and saying its three months.

examples.en: Ben rides a bicycle in spring.
examples.why: Im Frühling supplies the season; fährt … Fahrrad means rides a bicycle.

examples.de: Anna geht im Januar ins Museum.
examples.en: Anna goes to the museum in January.
examples.why: Im Januar supplies the month; ins Museum is a destination phrase.

references.title: All twelve months
references.note: All month names are masculine: der Januar, der Februar and so on. Ich reise im August means I travel in August. Ich arbeite am Montag uses am because Monday is a weekday, not a month.

references.title: Seasons in Germany, Austria and Switzerland
references.note: This three-month grouping is a simple seasonal calendar, not a weather promise. In D-A-CH, swimming and cycling are common warm-season activities. Ich fahre im Sommer Fahrrad gives one personal habit; Ich gehe im Winter ins Museum gives another, without claiming everyone does the same.

watch: Use im März and im Winter; use am Mittwoch for a weekday.

practice.prompt: Which group contains the three autumn months?
practice.explanation: Autumn is September through November in this learning calendar.

practice.prompt: Build: I travel in May.
practice.explanation: Im introduces a month.

practice.prompt: Complete: Ich schwimme ___ Sommer.
practice.explanation: A season takes im.

blind.prompt: Say “We travel in October.” Keep the order person, verb, time.
blind.explanation: Wir takes reisen; Oktober takes im.

retrieval.prompt: Name the month after Februar. Write only the German month.
retrieval.explanation: März is the third month.

retrieval.prompt: Say “I read in winter.” Begin Ich and use lesen.
retrieval.explanation: Ich takes lese; winter is im Winter.

retrieval.prompt: Write the three spring months in order, separated by commas.
retrieval.explanation: These are the spring months in the three-month calendar.

reading.title: Three seasonal hobbies
reading.text: Mira wohnt in der Schweiz. Sie fährt im April gern Fahrrad. Ben wohnt in Wien. Er schwimmt im August gern. Anna wohnt in Hamburg. Sie liest im November viel. Im Dezember geht sie ins Museum. Alle drei lernen Deutsch.
reading.translation: Mira lives in Switzerland. She likes riding a bicycle in April. Ben lives in Vienna. He likes swimming in August. Anna lives in Hamburg. She reads a lot in November. In December she goes to the museum. All three learn German.

questions.explanation: Sie fährt im April gern Fahrrad.

questions.prompt: Which season includes Ben’s swimming month?
questions.explanation: August is a summer month in the calendar.

questions.prompt: What does Anna do in December?
questions.explanation: Im Dezember geht sie ins Museum.

listening.title: Planning a seasonal trip
listening.text: Wann reist du, Leon? Im Februar. Ist das im Winter? Ja, genau. Und du, Mira? Ich reise im Juni. Das ist im Sommer. Am Montag planen wir die Reise zusammen. Im Juli arbeiten wir wieder.
listening.translation: When do you travel, Leon? In February. Is that in winter? Yes, exactly. And you, Mira? I travel in June. That is in summer. On Monday we plan the trip together. In July we work again.

questions.explanation: Leon answers Im Februar.
The speakers say Juni, then Das ist im Sommer.
Am Montag planen wir die Reise zusammen.

writing.prompt: Say two habits: you swim in June and you read in autumn. Use two sentences, each beginning Ich.
answers: Ich schwimme im Juni. Ich lese im Herbst.
writing.model: Ich schwimme im Juni. Ich lese im Herbst.
writing.hint: Use im before both Juni and Herbst.
writing.explanation: The month and season use the same time preposition.

Say when you cycle, using im Frühling.
Ask a partner when they travel; answer with a month.

examples.why: The season takes im.

title: Hear long and short vowels
goal: Use vowel length to distinguish familiar words and say a short sentence clearly.

objectives.title: Hear and produce long versus short German vowels
Mark vowel length and practice a short contrast

cards.title: Give the vowel enough time
cards.body: A vowel is an open mouth sound such as a, i or o. A long German vowel is held longer; a short one ends sooner and often sounds more relaxed. Keep a long vowel steady rather than sliding into a second English vowel. Length can distinguish words.

examples.why: The first a in Hafen is long: hold it. Compare the shorter first a in Hallo.
The i in Schiff is short; end it quickly before ff.

cards.title: Compare one sound at a time
cards.body: Say a pair slowly, then at normal speed. A written ie usually signals a long i; doubled consonants often signal a short vowel before them. A silent h can signal a long vowel. These are clues, not a rule for every word. Mark a long vowel with a line and a short one with a dot in your notes.

examples.why: Wohnen has long o, and sieben has long i, spelled ie.
Kommen has short o before mm, and Schiffe has short i before ff.

references.title: Useful length contrasts
rows: hold a in Hafen; shorten a in Hallo
keep wohnen steady; end kommen quickly
ie is long here; ff follows short i
references.note: Say sieben, Schiff: the first vowel lasts longer in sieben. Say wohnen, kommen: hold the first o only in wohnen. In Staat versus Stadt, both length and the final consonant group help distinguish the words.

references.title: A ten-second pronunciation loop
rows: Say just the target word slowly.
Say the whole sentence with the same vowel length.
references.note: Practice Das Schiff ist hier with short i rather than stretching it. Practice Sieben Schiffe sind hier with long i in sieben and short i in Schiffe. The loop trains a contrast, not just spelling.

terms.meaning: an open sound, for example a, i, o

watch: Do not turn every vowel into a long sound. The i in Schiff is short, while the ie in sieben is long.

practice.prompt: Which word has the long i sound?
practice.explanation: The spelling ie in sieben represents a long i.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence, then say long o in wohnen.
practice.explanation: Wir takes wohnen, whose first o is long.

practice.prompt: Choose Hafen or Hallo: which has the long first a? Write only the word.
practice.explanation: Hafen has a long first a; Hallo has a short first a.
practice.hint: Compare how long you hold the first vowel.

blind.prompt: Transfer the length clue: choose Miete or Mitte for the word with long i meaning “rent”. Type only the German word.
blind.explanation: The ie spelling in Miete signals the long i, unlike Mitte.

retrieval.prompt: Choose wohnen or kommen for the word with short o. Write only the word.
retrieval.explanation: The doubled mm follows the short o.

retrieval.prompt: Choose Staat or Stadt for the short-a word meaning “city”.
retrieval.explanation: Stadt has a short a and means city.

retrieval.prompt: Write “Seven ships are here.” Use German words for the number and plural. Then say long i followed by short i.
retrieval.explanation: Sieben has long i; Schiffe has short i.

reading.title: A pronunciation partner
reading.text: Mira und Ben lernen zusammen. Mira sagt: Hier ist ein Hafen. Ben sagt: Hallo, Mira! Dann liest Mira das Wort sieben. Ben liest Schiff. Beide sprechen langsam. Sie hören genau: Hafen hat ein langes a. Schiff hat ein kurzes i.
reading.translation: Mira and Ben study together. Mira says: Here is a port. Ben says: Hello, Mira! Then Mira reads the word seven. Ben reads ship. Both speak slowly. They listen carefully: Hafen has a long a. Schiff has a short i.

questions.prompt: Which word does Mira read after the greeting?
questions.explanation: Dann liest Mira das Wort sieben.
Beide sprechen langsam.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about Schiff?
questions.explanation: Schiff hat ein kurzes i.

listening.title: Three sounds to compare
listening.text: Wir wohnen hier. Sprechen Sie wohnen langsam: Das o ist lang. Jetzt kommen: Das o ist kurz. Hier sind sieben Schiffe. Sieben hat ein langes i. Schiffe hat ein kurzes i. Bitte sprechen Sie noch einmal.
listening.translation: We live here. Say wohnen slowly: The o is long. Now kommen: The o is short. Here are seven ships. Sieben has a long i. Schiffe has a short i. Please say it once again.

questions.explanation: The instruction says wohnen … Das o ist lang.
Hier sind sieben Schiffe.
Bitte sprechen Sie noch einmal.

writing.prompt: Write two sentences: “We live here. Seven ships are here.” Use Wir first, then Sieben.
answers: Wir wohnen hier. Sieben Schiffe sind hier.
writing.model: Wir wohnen hier. Sieben Schiffe sind hier.
writing.hint: Wohnen has long o; sieben has long i; Schiffe has short i.
writing.explanation: The written model gives three contrasting target sounds for speaking.

prompts: Say Hafen and Hallo; hold only the first a in Hafen.
Say wohnen and kommen with different vowel lengths.
Say seven ships in a complete sentence.

examples.why: Hold the o in wohnen without an English-style glide.
Keep sieben long and Schiffe short.

rubric: I hold the vowel longer in wohnen than in kommen.
I distinguish long i in sieben from short i in Schiff.
I keep the contrast when speaking the whole sentence.

examples.de: Das i in sieben ist lang.
examples.en: The i in sieben is long.

examples.de: Das i in Schiff ist kurz.
examples.en: The i in Schiff is short.

title: Read a simple city event notice
goal: Find an event, place and month using familiar words and names.

objectives.title: Use international words and visible names to read a tourist notice
Read about Hamburg as a northern German port city
Extract a place and time from an event notice

cards.title: Find words you already recognize
cards.body: An international word looks similar across languages, such as Hotel, Museum or Konzert. First scan a notice for these words, city names and month names. Then ask three small questions: what happens, where, and when? You can find useful information before understanding every word.

examples.de: Konzert im Museum: Hamburg, im Mai.
examples.en: Concert in the museum: Hamburg, in May.
examples.why: Konzert suggests the event, Museum the place, and im Mai the month.

examples.en: City tour in Hamburg: on Saturday.
examples.why: Hamburg is a visible name; am Samstag supplies the day.

cards.title: Use the known pieces as anchors
cards.body: Read a second time around the familiar words. Match one answer to each question instead of translating word by word. Hamburg is a northern German port city on the river Elbe. Harbour, river and concerts are useful settings for reading; the practice notices here are invented.

examples.de: Hamburg liegt in Norddeutschland. Die Elbe ist ein Fluss.
examples.en: Hamburg is in northern Germany. The Elbe is a river.
examples.why: The city name and Fluss help connect the place to its river.

examples.de: Anna hört im Juni ein Konzert in Hamburg.
examples.en: Anna listens to a concert in Hamburg in June.
examples.why: Anna answers who; Konzert answers what; Juni when; Hamburg where.

references.title: Three questions for a notice
references.note: Im Museum means in the museum; learn this location phrase whole for now. Konzert im Museum, im April gives where and when. Stadttour in Hamburg, am Sonntag gives a city and a weekday.

references.title: International word clues
references.note: A similar-looking word is a clue, not permission to guess the whole text. Museum names a place, but am Dienstag supplies a different kind of information: the day. Circle each clue, then verify it against the question you need to answer.

terms.meaning: look quickly for a particular detail

watch: Do not infer the day from a familiar place word. Find the actual am or im time phrase.

practice.prompt: Notice: “Festival in Hamburg, im September.” When is the festival?
practice.explanation: The time phrase is im September; Hamburg answers where.

practice.prompt: Build: The concert is in May.
practice.explanation: Put the known event first, then ist, then the time phrase.

practice.prompt: Notice: “Stadttour in Berlin, am Dienstag.” Write only the city name.
practice.explanation: In Berlin supplies the city; Dienstag is the weekday.

blind.prompt: Read the invented notice: “Konzert in Wien, im November.” Answer only the month question in a short German time phrase beginning Im.
blind.explanation: The phrase im November tells when; Wien tells where.

retrieval.prompt: Notice: “Museum in Hamburg, am Freitag.” Write only the city.
retrieval.explanation: Hamburg is the place name after in.

retrieval.prompt: Notice: “Festival in Berlin, im August.” Write the one German word naming the event.
retrieval.explanation: Festival names what happens.

retrieval.prompt: Notice: “Tour in Wien, am Sonntag.” Answer Wann? with a short phrase beginning Am.
retrieval.explanation: Am Sonntag is the day phrase.

reading.title: A city afternoon
reading.text: Hamburg liegt in Norddeutschland. Die Stadt hat einen Hafen. Die Elbe ist ein Fluss. Mira ist im Juli in Hamburg. Am Samstag hört sie ein Konzert. Am Sonntag macht sie eine Stadttour. Das Museum ist auch interessant. Ben liest die Information.
reading.translation: Hamburg is in northern Germany. The city has a port. The Elbe is a river. Mira is in Hamburg in July. On Saturday she listens to a concert. On Sunday she takes a city tour. The museum is interesting too. Ben reads the information.

questions.explanation: Die Elbe ist ein Fluss.

questions.prompt: When does Mira hear a concert?
questions.explanation: Am Samstag hört sie ein Konzert.

questions.prompt: What does she do on Sunday?
questions.explanation: Am Sonntag macht sie eine Stadttour.

listening.title: A new museum plan
listening.text: Hallo, Ben! Im Oktober bin ich in Wien. Am Freitag gehe ich ins Museum. Am Samstag ist ein Konzert im Theater. Gehen wir zusammen? Ja, gern. Das Museum ist interessant, und ich höre gern Musik.
listening.translation: Hello, Ben! I am in Vienna in October. On Friday I go to the museum. On Saturday there is a concert in the theatre. Shall we go together? Yes, gladly. The museum is interesting, and I like listening to music.

questions.prompt: Which city is the speaker in?
questions.explanation: The speaker says in Wien.
Am Freitag gehe ich ins Museum.
Ein Konzert im Theater gives the concert location.

writing.prompt: Use this notice: “Festival in Berlin, im März.” Write two short sentences: “The festival is in Berlin. The festival is in March.” Begin both Das Festival.
answers: Das Festival ist in Berlin. Das Festival ist im März.
writing.model: Das Festival ist in Berlin. Das Festival ist im März.
writing.hint: Use in with the city and im with the month.
writing.explanation: The two sentences separate where and when.

prompts: Name two international words from a city notice.
Read an invented notice aloud: Konzert in Berlin, im April.
Answer its Wo? and Wann? questions in short German phrases.

examples.why: The city answers Wo?
The month answers Wann?

rubric: I find an event word.
I distinguish a city from a time.
I answer from the actual notice.

examples.en: The city tour is on Monday.

title: Plan what to buy
goal: Plan a grocery purchase by saying what is needed and making a short shopping list

objectives.title: Plan a grocery purchase by saying what is needed and making a short shopping list
Name common foods, drinks and meals with their useful noun forms
Identify the main types of food shop and match purchases to them
Organize new vocabulary into meaningful groups before reviewing it

cards.title: Make a list for one meal
cards.body: Name the meal first, then name the things missing. Wir brauchen means we need. Group your list by the place you will buy each item. That lets you recover a forgotten word by imagining the shop.

examples.de: Zum Frühstück brauchen wir Brot und Butter.
examples.en: For breakfast we need bread and butter.
examples.why: Zum Frühstück sets the meal. Brauchen comes before wir when the meal comes first.

examples.de: Ich kaufe Brot in der Bäckerei.
examples.en: I buy bread at the bakery.
examples.why: A bakery sells baked goods, so Brot and Brötchen go together on the list.

cards.title: Work backwards from the shop
cards.body: Read a shopping note in two passes. First cross off what the household already has. Then group the remaining things by shop, or group them by foods and drinks. On the way home, cover the list and recall two things from each group.

examples.de: Wir haben Milch. Wir brauchen Eier.
examples.en: We have milk. We need eggs.
examples.why: Haben marks what is already there. Only eggs belong on the new list.

examples.de: Auf dem Markt kaufe ich Obst. In der Metzgerei kaufe ich Fleisch.
examples.en: I buy fruit at the market. I buy meat at the butcher’s.
examples.why: The places give two different cues for recalling a purchase.

references.title: Put a shopping note in order
rows: das Brot, das Brötchen, der Kuchen
das Fleisch, die Wurst, der Schinken
der Apfel, die Tomate, die Gurke
die Milch, das Wasser, der Reis
references.note: Need: Wir brauchen Brot. Already available: Wir haben Brot. Use the verb to decide whether bread goes on the list.

watch: Need: Wir brauchen Brot. Already available: Wir haben Brot. Use the verb to decide whether bread goes on the list.

practice.prompt: You already have milk. Which sentence adds eggs to the list?
practice.explanation: Brauchen identifies a need.

practice.prompt: Build: We buy bread at the bakery.
practice.explanation: After wir, kaufen keeps the -en ending.

practice.prompt: Which shop sells bread rolls? Write the German noun with its article.
practice.explanation: A Bäckerei specializes in baked goods.
practice.hint: Name the meal first, then name the things missing. Wir brauchen means we need. Group your list by the place you will buy each item. That lets you recover a forgotten word by imagining the shop.

blind.prompt: You have bread but need milk. Write two sentences beginning with Wir, first have and then need.
answers: Wir haben Brot. Wir brauchen Milch.
blind.explanation: Haben records the stock; brauchen adds the missing item.

retrieval.prompt: Say that you buy meat at the butcher’s, beginning Ich.
answers: Ich kaufe Fleisch in der Metzgerei.
retrieval.explanation: The shop is in der Metzgerei.

retrieval.prompt: Write: We need bread and eggs (in this order).
retrieval.explanation: A list joins items with und.

retrieval.prompt: Say that you buy fruit at the market, beginning Auf dem Markt.
answers: Auf dem Markt kaufe ich Obst.
retrieval.explanation: The place comes first, so the verb precedes ich.

reading.title: A note beside the fridge
reading.text: Morgen früh kommt Mia. Wir haben Brot und Käse, aber keine Milch. Ich kaufe Milch und Saft im Supermarkt. Jonas kauft Äpfel auf dem Markt. Wir essen zusammen in der Küche. Bitte kauf heute kein Brot!
reading.translation: Mia is coming tomorrow morning. We have bread and cheese, but no milk. I will buy milk and juice in the supermarket. Jonas will buy apples at the market. We will eat together in the kitchen. Please don’t buy bread today!

questions.explanation: Wir haben introduces the two things they already have.
Jonas kauft Äpfel names the shopper.
The note asks for no more bread because it is in stock.

listening.title: A voice message from the bus
listening.text: Hallo Pia, ich bin im Bus. Für das Abendessen brauchen wir Reis und Gemüse. Reis kaufe ich im Supermarkt. Kaufst du bitte Tomaten auf dem Markt? Milch haben wir noch. Bis später!
listening.translation: Hello Pia, I’m on the bus. For dinner we need rice and vegetables. I will buy rice in the supermarket. Could you buy tomatoes at the market? We still have milk. See you later!

questions.explanation: Für das Abendessen means for dinner.
She is asked to buy tomatoes auf dem Markt.
Milch haben wir noch says milk is still there.

writing.prompt: Write your list as two statements: we need bread; we buy bread at the bakery. Begin both with Wir.
answers: Wir brauchen Brot. Wir kaufen Brot in der Bäckerei.
writing.explanation: The first sentence names a need; the second gives the shop.
writing.model: Wir brauchen Brot. Wir kaufen Brot in der Bäckerei.
writing.hint: Read a shopping note in two passes. First cross off what the household already has. Then group the remaining things by shop, or group them by foods and drinks. On the way home, cover the list and recall two things from each group.

prompts: Tell a housemate what you already have.
Name two foods you need for breakfast.
Your housemate forgets the list. Remind them which shop to visit.
rubric: I distinguished haben and brauchen.
I named two foods without my notes.
My partner could match one food to its shop.

examples.de: Ich kaufe Brot in der Bäckerei.
examples.en: I buy bread at the bakery.
examples.why: A bakery sells baked goods, so Brot and Brötchen go together on the list.

examples.de: Wir haben Milch. Wir brauchen Eier.
examples.en: We have milk. We need eggs.
examples.why: Haben marks what is already there. Only eggs belong on the new list.

examples.en: The butter is in the fridge.

examples.de: Wir kaufen Brot in der Bäckerei.
examples.en: We buy bread at the bakery.

examples.de: In der Metzgerei gibt es Wurst.
examples.en: There is sausage at the butcher’s shop.

examples.de: Wir kaufen Obst auf dem Markt.
examples.en: We buy fruit at the market.
