title: Who buys what?
goal: Distinguish a sentence subject from a direct object and choose accusative articles

objectives.title: Distinguish a sentence subject from a direct object and choose accusative articles
Use common food and shopping verbs with a direct object

cards.title: Follow the shopping bag
cards.body: The subject does the buying. The direct object is the thing that goes in the bag. German marks this object with the accusative. For a masculine singular noun, der becomes den and ein becomes einen. With feminine, neuter and plural nouns, the article looks the same here.

examples.de: Der Apfel ist rot. Ich nehme den Apfel.
examples.en: The apple is red. I’ll take the apple.
examples.why: In the first sentence the apple is the subject; in the second ich is the subject and the apple is the object.

examples.de: Ich kaufe eine Gurke und ein Brot.
examples.en: I buy a cucumber and a loaf of bread.
examples.why: Gurke is feminine and Brot is neuter. Their indefinite articles keep the same form as objects.

cards.title: Change the shopping decision
cards.body: Ask what follows suchen (look for), kaufen (buy), nehmen (take) and brauchen (need). Each can point to a direct object. To rule something out, use keinen for a masculine singular object, keine for feminine or plural and kein for neuter.

examples.en: We are looking for a cheese.
examples.why: Der Käse is masculine. One unspecified cheese after suchen takes einen.

examples.de: Ich brauche keinen Saft, aber ich brauche Wasser.
examples.en: I don’t need any juice, but I need water.
examples.why: Der Saft has the negative object form keinen. Water as a substance can stand without an article.

references.title: Articles on the shopping list
references.note: Compare Der Salat ist frisch (the salad is fresh) with Ich nehme den Salat (I’ll take the salad). A plural has no equivalent of a/an.

watch: Compare Der Salat ist frisch (the salad is fresh) with Ich nehme den Salat (I’ll take the salad). A plural has no equivalent of a/an.

practice.prompt: Which sentence says ‘I’m looking for a salad’? (der Salat)
practice.explanation: The masculine object needs einen.

practice.prompt: Build: We buy the cheese.
practice.explanation: Der Käse becomes den Käse as a known direct object.

practice.prompt: Fill the article: Ich nehme ___ Brot. Use the for the neuter noun.
practice.explanation: Das Brot keeps das when it is an object.
practice.hint: The subject does the buying. The direct object is the thing that goes in the bag. German marks this object with the accusative. For a masculine singular noun, der becomes den and ein becomes einen. With feminine, neuter and plural nouns, the article looks the same here.

blind.prompt: You want the apple but no juice. Say ‘I take the apple. I do not buy any juice.’ Use nehmen and kaufen.
answers: Ich nehme den Apfel. Ich kaufe keinen Saft.
blind.explanation: Der Apfel changes to den and der Saft to keinen after the two object-taking verbs.

retrieval.prompt: Write: We need a salad.
retrieval.explanation: Salat is a masculine object.

retrieval.prompt: Write: I buy the cucumber.
retrieval.explanation: Feminine die stays die as an object.

retrieval.prompt: Write: I am looking for a loaf of bread. Use suchen and Brot.
retrieval.explanation: Neuter ein stays ein.

reading.title: At the little food stall
reading.text: Der Käse ist frisch. Lena kauft den Käse für das Abendessen. Sie nimmt auch eine Gurke, aber keinen Salat. Ihr Bruder sucht ein Brot. Der Verkäufer zeigt ihm das Brot. Saft haben die beiden schon zu Hause.
reading.translation: The cheese is fresh. Lena buys the cheese for dinner. She also takes a cucumber, but no salad. Her brother is looking for a loaf of bread. The seller shows him the bread. The two already have juice at home.

questions.explanation: Sie refers to Lena.
Keinen Salat rules out the salad.
Ein Brot is what he is looking for.

listening.title: Shopping for two
listening.text: Hallo, hier ist Eva. Ich suche einen Apfel für die Pause. Paul braucht eine Birne. Wir nehmen das Wasser, aber keinen Kaffee. Der Kaffee ist für Frau Baum. Sie zahlt später.
listening.translation: Hello, this is Eva. I’m looking for an apple for the break. Paul needs a pear. We’ll take the water, but no coffee. The coffee is for Ms Baum. She’ll pay later.

questions.explanation: Paul braucht eine Birne identifies him.

questions.prompt: What do Eva and Paul take to drink?
questions.explanation: Wir nehmen das Wasser.
Für Frau Baum identifies the recipient.

writing.prompt: Write two sentences: I’m looking for a cucumber. I’ll take the salad. Use suchen and nehmen.
answers: Ich suche eine Gurke. Ich nehme den Salat.
writing.explanation: Eine stays the same for Gurke. Den marks the masculine direct object.
writing.model: Ich suche eine Gurke. Ich nehme den Salat.
writing.hint: Ask what follows suchen (look for), kaufen (buy), nehmen (take) and brauchen (need). Each can point to a direct object. To rule something out, use keinen for a masculine singular object, keine for feminine or plural and kein for neuter.

prompts: Point to an apple and identify it with der.
Tell a shopkeeper you want that apple using nehmen.
Decline a juice and ask for a cucumber instead.
rubric: I named the masculine noun with der.
I changed der to den after nehme.
My negative article matched its object.

examples.de: Ich kaufe eine Gurke und ein Brot.
examples.en: I buy a cucumber and a loaf of bread.
examples.why: Gurke is feminine and Brot is neuter. Their indefinite articles keep the same form as objects.

examples.en: We are looking for a cheese.
examples.why: Der Käse is masculine. One unspecified cheese after suchen takes einen.

vocabulary.forms: ich suche, du suchst, hat gesucht
ich nehme, du nimmst, er nimmt, hat genommen
ich kaufe, du kaufst, hat gekauft

title: Ask for quantities and prices
goal: Request goods, ask where to find them, ask a price and complete a short shop exchange

objectives.title: Request goods, ask where to find them, ask a price and complete a short shop exchange
Use useful quantities and shopping units with food and drink
Identify the main types of food shop and match purchases to them

cards.title: Name the unit as well as the food
cards.body: In a shop, Ich möchte …, bitte politely asks for something. Use a unit such as ein Kilo, ein Liter or eine Flasche before the item. In everyday orders, food names follow the unit directly. For an amount of milk, say einen Liter Milch.

examples.de: Ich möchte ein Kilo Kartoffeln, bitte.
examples.en: I’d like a kilo of potatoes, please.
examples.why: Kilo is neuter. There is no German word for ‘of’ between Kilo and Kartoffeln.
Flasche counts containers, so two takes the plural Flaschen.

cards.title: Get the missing information
cards.body: Ask where something is with Wo finde ich …? To ask its price, match the verb to what is priced: Was kostet …? for one item and Was kosten …? for several. German prices use a decimal comma. At the till, Das ist alles means your order is complete.

examples.de: Wo finde ich den Reis? – Dort rechts.
examples.en: Where can I find the rice? – Over there on the right.
examples.why: Finde takes the masculine direct object den Reis; rechts tells you the direction.

examples.de: Was kosten die Tomaten? – Zwei Euro fünfzig.
examples.en: How much are the tomatoes? – Two euros fifty.
examples.why: Plural Tomaten takes kosten. The amount can be written 2,50 €.

references.title: How much do you want?
rows: one litre of milk as an object
references.note: Was kostet das Brot? asks the price of one loaf. Was kosten die Eier? asks about plural eggs. Cent can be omitted in Zwei Euro zehn (2,10 €).

watch: Was kostet das Brot? asks the price of one loaf. Was kosten die Eier? asks about plural eggs. Cent can be omitted in Zwei Euro zehn (2,10 €).

practice.prompt: What does eine Packung Reis mean?
practice.explanation: Packung identifies a packet.

practice.prompt: Build a polite price question for a loaf of bread.
practice.explanation: Das Brot is singular, so use kostet.

practice.prompt: Supply the verb: Was ___ die Äpfel?
practice.explanation: The plural Äpfel takes kosten.
practice.hint: In a shop, Ich möchte …, bitte politely asks for something. Use a unit such as ein Kilo, ein Liter or eine Flasche before the item. In everyday orders, food names follow the unit directly. For an amount of milk, say einen Liter Milch.

blind.prompt: Ask where to find the cheese. Then ask the price of the eggs, beginning Wo finde ich and Was kosten.
answers: Wo finde ich den Käse? Was kosten die Eier?
blind.explanation: Den Käse is the object of finde; die Eier is plural with kosten.

retrieval.prompt: Order one bottle of water using Ich möchte and bitte.
answers: Ich möchte eine Flasche Wasser, bitte.
retrieval.explanation: Eine Flasche names one container.

retrieval.prompt: Ask how much the salad costs.
retrieval.explanation: The salad is the subject of kostet.

retrieval.prompt: Say ‘Two kilos of potatoes, please.’
retrieval.explanation: Kilo stays unchanged as a measure after two.

reading.title: Shopping before the visitors arrive
reading.text: Im Laden kauft Eva zwei Flaschen Wasser und ein Kilo Kartoffeln. Die Kartoffeln kosten zwei Euro. Eva braucht auch Käse. Er ist links neben der Milch. Sie nimmt zweihundert Gramm. Dann geht sie zur Kasse.
reading.translation: In the shop Eva buys two bottles of water and a kilo of potatoes. The potatoes cost two euros. Eva also needs cheese. It is to the left of the milk. She takes two hundred grams. Then she goes to the till.

questions.prompt: How much water does Eva buy?
questions.explanation: Zwei Flaschen Wasser gives the count.
Die Kartoffeln kosten zwei Euro.

options: To the left of the milk
questions.explanation: Links neben der Milch gives its location.

listening.title: At a market counter
listening.text: Guten Morgen! Ich möchte ein halbes Kilo Tomaten und drei Äpfel, bitte. Was kostet das zusammen? Vier Euro zwanzig. Brauchen Sie eine Tüte? Nein, danke. Das ist alles. Auf Wiedersehen!
listening.translation: Good morning! I’d like half a kilo of tomatoes and three apples, please. How much is that altogether? Four euros twenty. Do you need a bag? No, thank you. That’s all. Goodbye!

questions.explanation: Drei Äpfel means three apples.
Vier Euro zwanzig gives €4.20.

questions.prompt: Does the shopper take a bag?
questions.explanation: The reply is Nein, danke.

writing.prompt: Order a litre of milk and close the sale: I would like a litre of milk, please. That is all.
answers: Ich möchte einen Liter Milch, bitte. Das ist alles.
writing.explanation: Möchte makes a polite request and einen is used for the masculine unit.
writing.model: Ich möchte einen Liter Milch, bitte. Das ist alles.
writing.hint: Ask where something is with Wo finde ich …? To ask its price, match the verb to what is priced: Was kostet …? for one item and Was kosten …? for several. German prices use a decimal comma. At the till, Das ist alles means your order is complete.

prompts: Ask where the potatoes are.
Order a quantity and ask what it costs altogether.
The seller offers a bag. Accept or decline and close the exchange.
rubric: I named both the amount and food.
I asked a price using kostet or kosten.
I responded to the final offer.

examples.why: Flasche counts containers, so two takes the plural Flaschen.

examples.de: Wo finde ich den Reis? – Dort rechts.
examples.en: Where can I find the rice? – Over there on the right.
examples.why: Finde takes the masculine direct object den Reis; rechts tells you the direction.

examples.en: I’d like a hundred grams of cheese.
How many grams do you need?
We need a litre of milk.
I’ll take a piece of cake.

vocabulary.forms: es kostet, sie kosten, hat gekostet

title: Offer a dish and explain a preference
goal: Offer food, accept or decline politely and respond to a meal greeting

objectives.title: Offer food, accept or decline politely and respond to a meal greeting
Say which foods and drinks you like and which you do not eat or drink
Use the present forms of essen and mögen and the polite request forms of möchten
Use food-related jobs and everyday meal politeness as German-speaking social contexts

cards.title: A preference or an offer?
cards.body: Ich mag Käse describes an ordinary preference. Ich möchte Käse is a request on this occasion. To offer something, turn the request around: Möchtest du …? Say Ja, gern to accept or Nein, danke to decline. At the start of a meal, Guten Appetit wishes the others an enjoyable meal.

examples.de: Ich mag Fisch, aber heute möchte ich Suppe.
examples.en: I like fish, but today I’d like soup.
examples.why: Mag tells the usual preference. Möchte names today’s choice.

examples.de: Möchtest du noch Salat? – Nein, danke, ich bin satt.
examples.en: Would you like more salad? – No thanks, I’m full.
examples.why: Noch offers more, while satt gives a polite reason for declining.

cards.title: Answer the person at the table
cards.body: Speak to a friend with Möchtest du …? and to a guest you address formally with Möchten Sie …? You can like something and still decline it. Use essen or trinken with gern for what you enjoy doing; set nicht before gern for a dislike.

examples.en: Enjoy your meal! – Thanks, you too!
examples.why: Gleichfalls returns the good wish to someone who is eating too.

examples.de: Ich trinke nicht gern Cola, aber ich esse gern Kuchen.
examples.en: I don’t like drinking cola, but I like eating cake.
examples.why: Gern goes with an action. Use trinken for drinks and essen for food.

references.title: Three useful verbs at the table
references.note: Ich mag Tee states a preference. Ich möchte Tee requests some now. At a toast you may hear Prost! or Zum Wohl!; before eating, Guten Appetit!

watch: Ich mag Tee states a preference. Ich möchte Tee requests some now. At a toast you may hear Prost! or Zum Wohl!; before eating, Guten Appetit!

practice.prompt: Which is a request for tea right now?
practice.explanation: Möchte expresses a wish on this occasion.

practice.prompt: Build an offer to one friend: Would you like more soup?
practice.explanation: The verb comes first in a yes/no offer.

practice.prompt: A friend who is also eating says Guten Appetit! Complete: Danke, ___.
practice.explanation: Gleichfalls returns the wish.
practice.hint: Ich mag Käse describes an ordinary preference. Ich möchte Käse is a request on this occasion. To offer something, turn the request around: Möchtest du …? Say Ja, gern to accept or Nein, danke to decline. At the start of a meal, Guten Appetit wishes the others an enjoyable meal.

blind.prompt: You are addressing a customer formally. Offer more coffee; then, as the customer, decline with ‘No, thanks’.
answers: Möchten Sie noch Kaffee? Nein, danke.
blind.explanation: Sie calls for möchten, and the second sentence declines the offer.

retrieval.prompt: Say ‘I like cheese’ using mögen.
retrieval.explanation: Ich takes mag.

retrieval.prompt: Ask a friend ‘Do you like fish?’ using mögen.
retrieval.explanation: Place magst before du.

retrieval.prompt: Say 'He likes eating soup' using essen and gern.
retrieval.explanation: Er takes the stem-changing isst.

reading.title: A small meal in the garden
reading.text: Mia und Jan essen im Garten. Mia mag Fisch und Salat. Heute möchte sie nur Salat, denn sie ist schon fast satt. Jan isst gern Brot mit Käse. Mia fragt: „Möchtest du noch Wasser?“ Jan sagt: „Ja, gern!“
reading.translation: Mia and Jan are eating in the garden. Mia likes fish and salad. Today she only wants salad because she is almost full. Jan likes eating bread with cheese. Mia asks whether he would like more water. Jan says yes, gladly.

questions.explanation: Mia mag introduces both foods.
Nur Salat restricts the current choice.
Ja, gern answers the water offer.

listening.title: A guest at lunch
listening.text: Guten Appetit, Herr Klein! Danke, gleichfalls. Möchten Sie noch Reis? Nein, danke. Ich bin satt. Der Reis schmeckt sehr gut. Möchten Sie einen Tee? Ja, gern, aber bitte ohne Zucker.
listening.translation: Enjoy your meal, Mr Klein! Thanks, you too. Would you like some more rice? No thanks. I’m full. The rice tastes very good. Would you like a tea? Yes, gladly, but without sugar, please.

questions.prompt: Why does the guest decline more rice?
questions.explanation: Ich bin satt gives his reason.
He answers Ja, gern to the tea offer.

questions.prompt: How does he want the drink?
questions.explanation: Ohne Zucker specifies no sugar.

writing.prompt: Write 'I like fish. Today I would like salad.' Use mögen and möchten and begin the second sentence Heute.
answers: Ich mag Fisch. Heute möchte ich Salat.
writing.explanation: Mag describes a usual preference. After Heute the verb comes before ich.
writing.model: Ich mag Fisch. Heute möchte ich Salat.
writing.hint: Speak to a friend with Möchtest du …? and to a guest you address formally with Möchten Sie …? You can like something and still decline it. Use essen or trinken with gern for what you enjoy doing; set nicht before gern for a dislike.

examples.en: Would you like more salad? – No thanks, I’m full.
examples.why: Noch offers more, while satt gives a polite reason for declining.

examples.en: Enjoy your meal! – Thanks, you too!

cards.title: Move the time; keep the verb
cards.body: In a German statement the changed verb belongs in position two. A whole time phrase counts as one position. Ich esse morgens Brot and Morgens esse ich Brot tell the same basic fact. Put morgens (in the mornings), mittags or abends first to organize a meal diary.

examples.why: Zum Frühstück is one time block. Trinke comes immediately after it and ich follows.

examples.de: Ich esse mittags Reis. Abends esse ich Suppe.
examples.en: I eat rice at midday. In the evenings I eat soup.
examples.why: When abends takes the first position, the subject moves behind esse.

cards.title: Read a food worker’s shift
cards.body: A cook, baker or seller may describe both a job and personal meals. Find the person with Wer?, the activity with Was?, the place with Wo? and the time with Wann? Build the answer around the changed verb and switch the time to the front to contrast shifts.

examples.de: Am Morgen backt Ada Brot. Sie ist Bäckerin.
examples.en: In the morning Ada bakes bread. She is a baker.
examples.why: Wann? Am Morgen. Wer? Ada. The time phrase is one unit before backt.

examples.de: Mittags kocht Tim im Restaurant. Abends isst er zu Hause.
examples.en: At midday Tim cooks in the restaurant. In the evening he eats at home.
examples.why: Wo? gives two different places; the opening time word tells which answer belongs to which action.

practice.explanation: Wo asks for a location.

blind.prompt: Write ‘In the mornings he drinks tea. In the evenings he eats fish.’ Begin with Morgens and Abends.
answers: Morgens trinkt er Tee. Abends isst er Fisch.
blind.explanation: Both times occupy position one. Er takes trinkt and isst.

retrieval.explanation: The verb stays second.

retrieval.prompt: Start with Zum Abendessen: I drink water for dinner.
retrieval.explanation: One meal phrase fills the first position.

retrieval.prompt: Ask in German ‘Where does Ada work?’
retrieval.explanation: The question word precedes the verb.

reading.title: A cook by the lake
reading.text: Nils arbeitet als Koch in einem kleinen Restaurant am See. Morgens kauft er Gemüse auf dem Markt. Mittags kocht er für die Gäste. Er selbst isst nachmittags eine Suppe. Abends trinkt er zu Hause Tee mit seiner Frau.
reading.translation: Nils works as a cook in a small restaurant by the lake. In the mornings he buys vegetables at the market. At midday he cooks for the guests. He himself eats a soup in the afternoon. In the evenings he drinks tea with his wife at home.

questions.prompt: Who is the meal at midday for?
questions.explanation: Für die Gäste identifies the recipients.
Nachmittags gives his own meal time.
Auf dem Markt answers Wo?.

listening.title: A baker explains her routine
listening.text: Ich heiße Vera und bin Bäckerin. Morgens backe ich Brötchen. Zum Frühstück esse ich Joghurt. Nachmittags trinke ich Kaffee mit meiner Schwester. Abends kochen wir zusammen Reis und Gemüse.
listening.translation: My name is Vera and I am a baker. In the mornings I bake bread rolls. For breakfast I eat yoghurt. In the afternoons I drink coffee with my sister. In the evenings we cook rice and vegetables together.

questions.explanation: Brötchen are bread rolls.

questions.prompt: What does she eat for breakfast?
questions.explanation: Zum Frühstück esse ich Joghurt tells us what she eats herself.
Mit meiner Schwester means with my sister.

writing.prompt: Write two time-first sentences: At midday I cook rice. In the evenings we eat bread. Use Mittags and Abends.
answers: Mittags koche ich Reis. Abends essen wir Brot.
writing.explanation: Koche and essen stand directly after the time words.
writing.model: Mittags koche ich Reis. Abends essen wir Brot.
